title: Training in Practice
html:
Most failed training runs are bugs or bad settings, not bad architectures. A short, disciplined routine — start small, overfit one batch, read the loss curves, then tune — finds problems quickly.

A debugging routine

1
Look at the data
Plot samples with their labels; check shapes, ranges, class balance, normalisation, and that inputs and labels still line up after shuffling.
2
Check the first loss
For k balanced classes it should be ≈ ln k. Far off → wrong loss, wrong labels or bad init.
3
Overfit one small batch
A healthy model + training loop drives the loss on 10–50 examples to ~0. If it can't, there's a bug.
4
Train a simple baseline
Small model, Adam(W) at 1e-3, no fancy tricks. Get something working end-to-end.
5
Scale up and regularise
Bigger model, more data, augmentation, schedules — one change at a time, tracking validation metrics.

Reading loss curves

What you seeDiagnosisTry
Train ↓, validation ↓ then ↑OverfittingEarly stopping, regularisation, augmentation, more data
Both high and flatUnderfitting or LR too lowBigger model, higher LR, train longer, check for bugs
Loss jumps to nan / infExploding gradients, LR too high, log(0)Lower LR, gradient clipping, warmup, check the loss inputs
Very noisy lossLR too high or batch too smallLower LR, larger batch, LR decay
Validation better than trainingDropout/augmentation only in training — or a leaky validation setUsually fine; check for leakage
Plateau, then sudden dropPoor init or LR schedule kicking inWarmup, better init

Hyper-parameter tuning

PriorityHyper-parameterTypical search
1Learning rateLog scale: 1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3…
2Batch size / schedule / epochsAs large as memory allows; cosine + warmup
3Weight decay, dropout0–0.1; 0–0.5
4Architecture (depth, width)Scale up until validation stops improving
Key point

Prefer random search over grid search (it explores important dimensions better), sample learning rates on a log scale, and tune on a smaller budget before full runs. Tools such as Optuna or Ray Tune automate this; Weights & Biases or TensorBoard track the runs.

Mixed precision

Running most operations in 16-bit floats (float16 or bfloat16) halves memory and uses fast tensor cores, with little accuracy loss. torch.autocast picks the precision per operation — matrix multiplies in 16-bit, sensitive reductions in 32-bit.

GPU memory and gradient accumulation

Memory holds weights, gradients, optimizer state (Adam: 2× weights) and the activations saved for backprop, which grow with batch size. When a batch doesn't fit, accumulate gradients over several micro-batches before stepping:

Speed-upHow
Keep the GPU fednum_workers > 0, pin_memory=True, avoid .item() / .cpu() inside the loop
Mixed precisiontorch.autocast + bf16/fp16
Compilemodel = torch.compile(model) fuses operations
Bigger batchesBetter hardware use (retune the LR)
Multiple GPUsDistributedDataParallel (DDP); FSDP to shard huge models
Save memoryGradient checkpointing (recompute activations), smaller batch + accumulation
Your loss isn't decreasing. How do you debug it?

Check the data and labels first, then the initial loss against ln k, then try to overfit a single small batch. If that fails, look for bugs: missing zero_grad, softmax before CrossEntropyLoss, wrong label dtype/shape, frozen parameters, forgetting optimizer.step(), or an LR that's far too high or low. Then inspect gradient norms per layer.

What is mixed precision training?

Doing most computation in 16-bit floats while keeping a 32-bit master copy of the weights. It cuts memory and speeds up training on tensor-core GPUs. With float16 a gradient scaler prevents small gradients from underflowing; bfloat16 has float32's range and usually doesn't need one.
